candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Determine a least common denominator and rewrite unlike fractions as equivalent fractions with that denominator before subtracting.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: All three experts describe the same preparatory step of creating equivalent fractions with a shared denominator before subtraction.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Rewrite a number into a more workable equivalent form, such as converting a mixed number with an improper fraction part into standard mixed-number form or simplifying a starting fraction part before subtraction.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: A's broader normalization skill overlaps with B and C's normalization of improper mixed forms and simplified starting fraction forms; the shared core is rewriting an operand into a more workable equivalent form before subtraction.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Represent whole numbers and mixed numbers in aligned whole-part and fraction-part form so corresponding parts can be subtracted.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: B and C explicitly separate alignment of whole and fractional parts, especially rewriting a whole number as a whole plus 0 over a denominator. A folds this behavior into its broader normalization skill rather than isolating it.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Carry out subtraction once forms are aligned, including subtracting numerators of like fractions and, in mixed-number problems, subtracting whole parts and fraction parts separately.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: A states the operation more broadly, including whole-part subtraction in mixed numbers, while B and C isolate the like-fraction subtraction step. These represent the same core subtraction operation after alignment, with A at slightly broader granularity.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Borrow 1 from the whole-number part and convert it into fractional units when the fractional subtraction would otherwise be negative or cannot be completed directly.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: All three experts describe the same borrowing/regrouping process of converting one whole into denominator-over-denominator units to support mixed-number subtraction.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Reduce a fraction or mixed-number result to lowest terms, including recognizing when a zero fractional part simplifies to a whole number or zero.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: A separates simplification as its own skill, whereas B and C combine simplification with final composition into a single end-of-solution skill.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Combine the computed whole and fractional parts and express the answer in an appropriate final form, including a mixed number, fraction, integer, or zero.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: A isolates final recombination/presentation of the answer as a distinct skill, while B and C merge this with final simplification.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Combine the computed whole and fractional parts and express the final answer in lowest terms, including reducing to an integer or zero when appropriate.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: B and C treat final composition and simplification as one integrated end-of-problem skill. A splits this same region into two separate skills, so no single A skill maps exactly to this combined concept.

alignment_summary: The three codebooks align strongly on common denominator, normalization, subtraction, and regrouping. The main structural difference is granularity: Expert A separates simplification and final composition, while Experts B and C combine them into one finalization skill; B and C also isolate mixed-number alignment as a separate preparatory skill, whereas A includes much of that behavior inside normalization.
